chapter_theme: The lament gathers its themes: lying like a discarded corpse, wandering without caste as Kapila's agama says, casting off the bellows-body and the births as stone, tree, fish, bird and grass, waiting ripe for grace, the house of great bliss, the fullness seen in all inner speech, being dead without dying under the true guru's feet, the Lord as the string that makes the puppet dance, the reality no reading, speech or worship shows, and then the breath in cipher: the twelve-legged horse bound in two chains, the middle leg between the two outer ones, the wind-cow tied to the milk, the homa fire within, the three lights lit in the inner house and the dance seen in the heart, the centre of nada's end, and the sky known as open space.
structure_note: Loose runs: 126 to 130 on corpse, caste, body and births; 131 to 137 on grace, tattva, the centre, the house of bliss, fullness, the arts and birth cut off; 138 to 142 on madness, the living dead, the puppeteer, the hidden Lord and the unshown reality; 143 to 150 in cipher on the breath (horse, legs, cow, moon-boundary, fire, lights, nada's end, open sky). 126 is a near-double of 23 in the same work.

126.reading: When will I keep the thought that has ceased, lie like a discarded corpse with the inner bone turned white bone, and see?
126.nuance: ஒழிந்த கருத்து is thought that has stopped, or the one thought that remains when the rest have gone; the near-double at 23 has ஒழிந்த தருமம் instead. வெள் எலும்பு, the bone bleached white, is the corpse long dead; the poet asks to lie as one while still seeing (காண்பது), the living death of 89 and 139.

127.reading: When will I go about without any division of caste, as the words of the agama spoken by the first Kapila say?
127.nuance: ஆதிகபிலர் is Kapila, the Sankhya sage whom the Siddhar lists count as one of their own; the ஆகமம் credited to him is unidentified, and the Tamil Kapilar Agaval, the best-known verse attack on caste, may be meant. The verse grounds castelessness in a text, which is unusual for a Siddhar, who more often grounds it in the body.

128.reading: When will I mark gambling, theft and the chain of karma, throw off this bellows that the wind blows, and reach you?
128.nuance: காற்று ஊதும் துருத்தி, the bellows the wind blows, is the breathing body, the Siddhars' recurring figure. சுட்டி may be 'pointing out' (naming the faults to be left) or 'branding, burning' them; தொடர்வினை, karma that follows, is the third item beside the two vices.

129.reading: When will I stand united in the lamp of the sounding bell, instead of perishing caught in the net of desire, the bond?
129.nuance: ஆசைவலைப் பாசம் makes desire itself the net and the bond (pasam). ஓசைமணித் தீபம், the lamp of the bell's sound, joins the two inner signs of the yoga tradition, nada heard and light seen, into one object to merge with.

130.reading: When will I say 'enough' to the births I have been born into as stone, tree, fish, bird and grass?
130.nuance: The list runs across the kinds of life, with stone (கல்) first, so that even the inert is a birth. போதும் என்பது, saying 'enough', is the only act asked for; the verse does not say what ends the births, only that the poet should be sated with them.

131.reading: When will I rest on no object that suits me, and in thought, ripe, watch for your grace?
131.nuance: பக்குவம், ripeness, is the Saiva term for the soul ready to receive grace; the verse pairs it with holding to nothing. பார்த்திருப்பது is waiting and watching, not acting: grace is expected, not earned.

132.reading: When will I understand, in harmony with its root, the tattva that comes swaying and whirling with its base?
132.nuance: தூர் is a plant's base or stump, so தூரோடு அசைந்து is 'swaying with its base' and வேரோடு இசைந்து 'in accord with its root', the tattva as a plant to be known from the root up; தூர் can also be read as distance, 'moving from afar'. The verse asks to understand the tattvas, not to discard them.

133.reading: When will I set at the single central root the picture that arose in fear, its parts displaced from the centre?
133.nuance: சித்திரம், the picture, is unexplained: the body, the mind's images, or the yantra; பாகம் நடு மாறி, its parts shifted from the middle, is read by the yoga tradition as the breath gone into the side channels, and ஏக நடு மூலம், the one central root, as the base of the sushumna. பயந்து எழுந்த, risen from fear or born from, is itself two readings.

134.reading: When will I go by the high street of knowledge that shows one joy, see the house of great bliss and possess it?
134.nuance: ஓரின்பம் and பேரின்பம், the one joy and the great joy, are graded: the road of knowledge shows a single joy and the house at its end is the great one. The house (வீடு) is release, as at 102.

135.reading: When will I see as fullness all that came as cause and spoke in my thought, and praise it?
135.nuance: காரணமாய் வந்து, coming as cause, and உரைத்தது, what spoke, point to the inner speaking of the Lord or guru in the mind; the verse asks to see all of it as பூரணம், the fullness, rather than as separate instructions. 114 saw the fullness above the point; here it is heard.

136.reading: When will I see, after examining all the arts that are studied, the truth in which there is never a 'you'?
136.nuance: நீ என்றும் இல்லா நிசம் is the hinge: 'the truth in which there is no you', that is, no second person and no duality, or 'the truth that you are never not', the Lord's constant presence. The arts (கலை) are examined to the end and found not to be it, as at 99; the verse does not despise them.

137.reading: When will I take as my aim the Lord who gave the clan, join him without parting, and cut off birth?
137.nuance: குலம் அளித்த நாயகன் is the Lord who gave the lineages (the maker of clans), or who gave the poet a kin, the devotees; after 127 has refused caste, the only clan is the one he gives. குறியாகக் கொண்டு, taking as target or sign, is the yogi's fixing of attention.

138.reading: When will I stand seized by madness and have your grace, like those who dance in frenzy when the possession takes them?
138.nuance: மருள் ஆடுவார் are the possessed dancers of village worship, and மத்து the frenzy that comes on them (or the churning-stick, which is unlikely here); பித்து, madness, is the Siddhars' name for their own state, taken up from 125. Grace is to be had in a seizure, not in composure.

139.reading: When will I ask to be dead without dying, cooked without being cooked, under the golden feet of the true guru?
139.nuance: The two paradoxes, சாவாமல் செத்து and வேகாமல் வெந்து, are Siddhar formulas for the body kept while the self is gone, and for austerity that burns without consuming. Both happen at the guru's feet; the verse makes even the asking (வேண்டுவது) something to wait for.

140.reading: When will I know you, the string that makes me dance while I stay not knowing myself, and gain tapas?
140.nuance: சூத்திரம் is the puppet's string and the puppeteer's device; the poet dances by it unknowing, and knowing the string is knowing the Lord. The figure returns at 150 as a kite-string, free.

141.reading: When will my thieving mind clear and see the Lord who stayed hidden, unknown to the heart?
141.nuance: உள்ளம் and கள்ள மனம் repeat the pun of 76 (உள்ளக் கருத்து, கள்ளக் கருத்து): the Lord hides in the heart that does not know him, and the deceitful mind must clear (தெளிந்து) before the hidden one is seen.

142.reading: When will I see the reality that is not seen by reading, not spoken by opening the mouth, and does not appear by worship?
142.nuance: Three means are denied in turn, scripture (வாசித்தும்), speech and ritual worship (பூசித்தும்); the verse does not say what does show the reality, only that these do not. The denial of worship is the sharpest for a devotional poet.

143.reading: When will I bind the twelve-legged horse that leaps, so that it does not kick the plate, within the two chains behind?
143.nuance: A cipher verse. The horse with twelve legs is the breath (Tirumular's ஈராறு கால் புரவி), its twelve being the twelve finger-breadths the breath travels or the twelve kalas; the two chains behind are, in the tradition, ida and pingala, or the two nostrils; சில்லம் is unexplained (a shard, a wheel, a plate). The plain sense is a wild horse tethered; the cipher makes it the breath held.

144.reading: When will I leave the two country legs, go through the middle leg, and sit within the two goat legs?
144.nuance: Wholly in cipher. நாட்டுக்கால் (the two legs planted in the country), நடுவுக்கால் (the middle leg) and ஆட்டுக்கால் (the two goat legs) are read by the tradition as ida and pingala, the sushumna, and a pair at the upper end (the two brows or two eyes, the 'moving' pair); 96 says the first two plainly. The plain words give a man stepping between legs of unlike kinds, which is not a sentence, so the cipher is the only reading.

145.reading: When will I fasten the taste of milk, set it in the place and cherish it, drive the wind-cow there and tie it?
145.nuance: காற்பசு, the wind-cow (காற்று பசு), is the breath; பால், milk, is the nectar of 97; பதி is the place, the town, or the Lord. The tradition reads it as the breath driven to the crown and bound where the nectar is; plainly it is a cow tied where it is fed. கட்டி வப்பது is கட்டி வைப்பது.

146.reading: When will I meet straight, going through the moon's boundary, instead of letting the mind run loose to many places and not watching it?
146.nuance: நிலவரை splits two ways: நிலா வரை, the moon's region or boundary (the moon-hall of 97, at the crown), or நில வரை, the limit of the land. With the cipher of the surrounding verses the first is likelier; நேர்படுவது, meeting straight or coming into line, is the mind's arrival after its scattering.

147.reading: When will I kindle the homa fire and stay within, so as to cross the sea of desire and climb the shore?
147.nuance: ஓமக் கனல், the fire of the oblation, is kindled உள், within: the Vedic fire is made inner, the yogic fire at the base that the Siddhars set against the outer rite. The sea of desire is crossed by burning, not by swimming.

148.reading: When will I light the three dawn-lights in the inner house and see the holy dance in the heart?
148.nuance: சுடர் மூன்று are the three lights, sun, moon and fire, which the tradition places in the body as the three channels or the three eyes; உள்வீடு is the body as house. The dance of Chidambaram is moved to the heart, the body replacing the hall.

149.reading: When will I cross all Vedanta and Veda by climbing into the house, and be at the central root of nada's end?
149.nuance: வேதாந்த வேதம் எல்லாம் are passed (கடந்து), not refuted: the texts are a stage before the house (வீடு, release) and before நாதாந்தம், the end of sound, where the yogi stands. மூல நடு, the central root, places even that end in the body.

150.reading: When will I know the sky as cut-open space, like a kite-string that flies and dances when the kite is gone and its loop torn?
150.nuance: பட்டம் is the kite and காது its ear or loop; with both gone the சூத்திரம், the string, flies free, and the simile is for the self loosed from what it carried. The same word was the puppet-string at 140 that made the poet dance; here the string dances by itself. வெட்ட வெளி, the open, cut-clear space, is the Siddhars' word for the final emptiness.

links.note: The Kural says birth is alike for all living beings and distinction comes only from the work they do; Pattirakiriyar asks to go about with no division of caste, as Kapila's agama says. Both deny caste by birth; the Kural keeps a distinction by deeds that the pulambal does not mention.

Sivavakkiyar asks the Siddhars what mind, soul, Shakti, Siva, caste-difference, release and root mantras are, in the seedless seed; Pattirakiriyar wants to live without caste-division on a text's authority. Both refuse caste, Sivavakkiyar by dissolving it with everything else and Pattirakiriyar by citing Kapila.

Earlier in the work the body is a rice-bellows carried about until one withers, to be thrown off to reach the Lord; here it is the bellows the wind blows, thrown off with gambling, theft and karma. The same bellows, filled with food in one and with breath in the other.

Pambatti's body is a torn bellows with nine gates into which the great wind entered, which is how speech arose, food for the burning ground for those who do not know the Lord; Pattirakiriyar's is the bellows the wind blows, to be cast off. Both make the breath in the body a wind in a leather bag.

Tirumular hears the ringing bell as the lamp of the inner breath, the body dazes, and he sees the hall; Pattirakiriyar asks to stand united in the lamp of the sounding bell. Both fuse the heard bell and the seen lamp into one inner object.

The Arutpulambal asks the Lord of Kannivanam whether the days spent as grass and shrub, as stone and tree, are not enough; Pattirakiriyar asks when he will say 'enough' to births as stone, tree, fish, bird and grass. The same list and the same word, போதும், as a reproach to the Lord in one and a hope for oneself in the other.

Arunagirinathar asks not to wander born as sparrow, kite, jackal, beast, worm, fish, elephant and tree; Pattirakiriyar wants to be done with births as stone, tree, fish, bird and grass. Both run through the kinds of life as a weariness, and the pulambal adds the inert stone.

The Kural says to cling to the clinging of the one without clinging, in order to let clinging go; Pattirakiriyar rests on no object and keeps only the watch for grace. Both leave a single hold when every other is dropped.

99 asks to live in the reality the chattering arts cannot reach; 136 adds the step of examining all the arts to the end first, and names what is seen after them, the truth with no 'you' in it. The arts are not skipped but exhausted.

The Kural says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births and the rest cannot; Pattirakiriyar asks to join the Lord without parting and so cut off birth. Both make attachment to the Lord the one means of ending rebirth.

Tirumular's Siva-gnanis wander as the dead while senses and body remain intact, unlike the purifiers and the monkey-glad knowers; Pattirakiriyar asks to be dead without dying under the true guru's feet. The same living death, as a class description in one and a petition in the other.

Kudhambai asks what the darkness of desire is to those who have been cooked without being cooked and seen the open space; Pattirakiriyar asks to be cooked without being cooked beneath the guru's feet. The formula வேகாமல் வெந்து is shared, a finished state in one and a hope in the other.

Tirumular says the Lord makes the elements dance as a deed makes a false puppet dance, and so brings the soul to awareness; Pattirakiriyar calls the Lord the string that makes him dance while he does not know himself. Both put the Lord behind the puppet, and both make knowing the hand the way out.

Sivavakkiyar asks the sastra-reciter whether the Veda will help when the death-sweat comes, and sets a moment's inner knowing against the whole bag of scripture; Pattirakiriyar names the reality that reading, speaking and worship do not show. Both deny that recitation reaches it.

Arunagirinathar's reality cannot be spoken by debaters, reached by the path of books or by imagined meditation; Pattirakiriyar's is not seen by reading, spoken by the mouth or shown by worship. The same three denials, with worship added by the pulambal.

Tirumular says that if you can tie the horse that rose with twelve legs so that it does not escape, and drink deeply, the body will not leave for thousands of years; Pattirakiriyar asks to bind the leaping twelve-legged horse in the two chains. The same ciphered horse; the Tirumanthiram names the gain (the body kept) that the pulambal leaves unsaid.

Sivavakkiyar says that if one stands the twelve legs still and reaches the five colours, the soul stays within the space and works in the head, and the inquirer becomes Brahman; Pattirakiriyar asks to bind the twelve-legged horse. Two Siddhars with the same count of legs for the breath, and the same stilling.

96 names the three channels plainly, the sushumna moving between ida and pingala, and asks to stand there unobstructed; 144 says the same thing in cipher, leaving the two outer legs and going by the middle one. Set side by side, the plain verse is the key to the coded one.

The Kural's woman says the sea of love certainly exists and the raft to cross it certainly does not; Pattirakiriyar means to cross the sea of desire and climb the shore by kindling the inner homa fire. The same காமக் கடல், the lover's with no way across, the ascetic's crossed by fire.

Tirumular says that when bindu and nada join and meet the moon, nectar wells up and the mantra rising there becomes the oblation; Pattirakiriyar kindles the homa fire within. Both move the sacrifice inside the body, the pulambal keeping the fire and the Tirumanthiram keeping the offering.

Tirumular's dancer has space for his body, the eight directions for hands and the three lights for his three eyes, and dances in the hall of the great body; Pattirakiriyar lights the three lights in the inner house and sees the dance in the heart. Both relocate the dance of the hall into a body lit by sun, moon and fire.

Nondi Siddhar beholds the master's holy dance in the light-space between the eyes, in the middle of the nose-tip, and gains the state of silence; Pattirakiriyar asks to see the holy dance in the heart with the three lights lit within. The dance is inward in both, placed at the brow by one and in the heart by the other.

Tirumular puts the good lady, good yoga, the aim and the Lord himself at the end of nada; Pattirakiriyar asks to be at the central root of nada's end, past all Vedanta and Veda. Both make the end of sound the yogi's station, and the pulambal adds that the texts are what is passed to reach it.

Kanjamalai Siddhar tells the mind that runs about to be caught and corrected and set within the open space of nada's end; Pattirakiriyar asks to stand at the root-centre of nada's end. The same place named in the same term, with the mind's capture as the means in one and the passing of scripture in the other.

At 140 the சூத்திரம் is the string by which the Lord makes the unknowing poet dance; at 150 it is the kite-string that flies and dances on its own once the kite and its loop are gone. The same word for the thread, bound to a hand in one and loose in the open sky in the other.

source_issues: 126 is a near-double of 23 (siddhar:meynjanap-pulambal:22): the second lines are the same and the first differ only in கருத்தினை / தருமத்தினை; one is probably a variant of the other carried into the running text.
145 line 2 கட்டி வப்பது for கட்டி வைப்பது.
143 line 1 சில்லம் is unexplained and may be corrupt.
